title: The Gibonacci Gelin–Cesàro Identity — Lifting the Degree-Four Product to Horadam Sequences
description: The parent entry (fibonacci-identities-oq-04-oq-01) lifted Vajda's master identity — and with it Cassini and Catalan — from the Fibonacci numbers to arbitrary integer Gibonacci (Horadam) sequences G(n) = a·Fₙ + b·Fₙ₋₁, replacing the sign constant (−1)^|n| by the characteristic discriminant μ = a² − ab − b². It also proved the Fibonacci Gelin–Cesàro identity Fₙ₋₂·Fₙ₋₁·Fₙ₊₁·Fₙ₊₂ − Fₙ⁴ = −1, but left the degree-four identity itself at the Fibonacci level. This entry closes that gap: it proves the Gibonacci Gelin–Cesàro identity G(n−2)·G(n−1)·G(n+1)·G(n+2) − G(n)⁴ = −μ², driven by the parent's own Gibonacci Cassini and Gibonacci Catalan (r = 2) identities. The mechanism is the same difference of squares that gives the Fibonacci case: Gibonacci Cassini (recentred) gives G(n−1)·G(n+1) = G(n)² + (−1)^|n|·μ and the Gibonacci Catalan r = 2 instance gives G(n−2)·G(n+2) = G(n)² − (−1)^|n|·μ, whose product is (G(n)²)² − ((−1)^|n|·μ)² = G(n)⁴ − μ². The odd-in-n sign factor (−1)^|n| is annihilated by the difference of squares, leaving the clean index-independent constant −μ². Two corollaries specialise the result: (a,b)=(1,0) gives μ=1 and recovers the Fibonacci identity (−1); (a,b)=(1,2) gives μ=−5 and yields the Lucas identity L(n−2)·L(n−1)·L(n+1)·L(n+2) − L(n)⁴ = −25. Everything is over Int.fib at all integer indices. Fully verified: 0 sorries, 0 axioms, no native_decide.

overview.historicalContext: The Gelin–Cesàro identity (proposed by E. Gelin, proved by E. Cesàro in the 1880s) Fₙ₋₂Fₙ₋₁Fₙ₊₁Fₙ₊₂ − Fₙ⁴ = −1 is a fourth-degree relative of Cassini's identity, obtained by multiplying two product identities. A. F. Horadam's generalized Fibonacci ('Gibonacci') sequences (1961) satisfy the same recurrence G(n+2)=G(n+1)+G(n) with arbitrary seeds, and over ℤ have the closed form G(n)=a·Fₙ+b·Fₙ₋₁. For such a sequence every product identity carries the characteristic μ = G(1)²−G(0)G(1)−G(0)² = a²−ab−b² in place of the Fibonacci unit constant — for the Lucas numbers μ = −5, the negated discriminant of x²−x−1. The parent entry lifted Vajda, Cassini, and Catalan to the Gibonacci level but proved Gelin–Cesàro only for the Fibonacci numbers; this entry completes the lift, showing the degree-four identity becomes G(n−2)G(n−1)G(n+1)G(n+2) − G(n)⁴ = −μ², all over the two-sided integer sequence so it holds at negative indices.
overview.problemStatement:
**Open direction (extending fibonacci-identities-oq-04-oq-01)**: the parent lifted Cassini and Catalan to Gibonacci sequences with the discriminant μ = a²−ab−b² but proved the Gelin–Cesàro identity only at the Fibonacci level. Prove the Gibonacci analogue.

**Result**: gib_gelin_cesaro — G(n−2)·G(n−1)·G(n+1)·G(n+2) − G(n)⁴ = −(a²−ab−b²)² for the Gibonacci sequence gib a b n = a·Fₙ + b·Fₙ₋₁ — together with its Fibonacci specialisation (μ=1, =−1) and Lucas specialisation (μ=−5, =−25).
overview.text: A Gibonacci sequence G(n)=a·Fₙ+b·Fₙ₋₁ has characteristic μ=a²−ab−b². The Gibonacci Gelin–Cesàro identity multiplies the recentred Cassini factor G(n−1)G(n+1)=G(n)²+(−1)^|n|μ by the Catalan r=2 factor G(n−2)G(n+2)=G(n)²−(−1)^|n|μ, a difference of squares whose cross term (the odd-in-n sign (−1)^|n|) cancels, leaving G(n)⁴−μ². Fibonacci (a,b)=(1,0) has μ=1 (the classical −1); Lucas (a,b)=(1,2) has μ=−5 (giving −25).
overview.proofStrategy:
**Proof Strategy.**

1. **Recentre Gibonacci Cassini.** Apply the parent's gib_cassini at base n−1 and normalise indices to obtain G(n)² − G(n−1)·G(n+1) = (−1)^|n−1|·μ. The lemma sign_flip n rewrites (−1)^|n−1| = −(−1)^|n|, giving G(n−1)·G(n+1) = G(n)² + (−1)^|n|·μ.
2. **Gibonacci Catalan, r = 2.** Apply gib_catalan at base n−2 with r=2; with Int.fib 2 = 1 and two sign-flips ((−1)^|n−2| = (−1)^|n|) this yields G(n−2)·G(n+2) = G(n)² − (−1)^|n|·μ.
3. **Difference of squares.** Multiply the two factors: (G(n)² − (−1)^|n|μ)·(G(n)² + (−1)^|n|μ) = (G(n)²)² − ((−1)^|n|μ)². Since ((−1)^|n|)² = 1, the sign disappears and the bracket equals G(n)⁴ − μ².
4. **Conclude.** A short calc reorders the four-factor product into the two Cassini/Catalan factors, substitutes, and a single linear_combination of the sign-square identity closes the goal at −μ² = −(a²−ab−b²)².
5. **Specialise.** gib 1 0 = Int.fib (μ=1) gives the Fibonacci identity (−1); lucas = gib 1 2 (μ=−5) gives the Lucas identity (−25), each by `simpa`/`norm_num` on the master result.
keyInsights: **The degree-four constant is exactly −μ².** Where the Fibonacci Gelin–Cesàro constant is the bare −1, the Gibonacci version is −μ² with μ = a²−ab−b² the same discriminant that controls the parent's Cassini/Catalan/Vajda identities. Fibonacci is μ=1 (−1); Lucas is μ=−5 (−25): the Lucas discriminant 5 reappears, squared.

**The odd sign factor cancels by difference of squares.** Cassini and the Catalan r=2 instance carry the same magnitude (−1)^|n|·μ with opposite signs; pairing them as (X−s)(X+s) annihilates the index-dependent term s=(−1)^|n|μ, which is precisely why the answer is a clean constant rather than a sign-alternating quantity.

**No new induction — the parent's Gibonacci infrastructure suffices.** The whole proof is a difference of squares over two instances of the parent's gib_cassini and gib_catalan plus the parity sign-flip; the Gibonacci lift of Gelin–Cesàro needs nothing beyond what the parent already built for Vajda.

**Faithful parallel of the Fibonacci proof.** The argument mirrors the parent's fib_gelin_cesaro line for line, with gib in place of Int.fib and the constant μ in place of 1 — demonstrating that the Gibonacci generalisation is structural, not ad hoc.

**Gelin–Cesàro is literally the square of Cassini's defect.** The degree-two Cassini and Catalan (r=2) identities carry the index-dependent defect ±(−1)^|n|·μ; the degree-four Gelin–Cesàro constant is exactly −(that defect)² = −μ², so the whole product hierarchy is powers of the single discriminant μ = a²−ab−b². That μ is (minus) the value on the seed (a,b) of the quadratic form attached to the characteristic polynomial x²−x−1, whose discriminant is 5 — the field discriminant of ℚ(√5). This is why the Lucas seed (1,2) gives μ = −5 and the Lucas constant is −25 = −5²: the discriminant, squared.

sections.title: The Flagship Statement and Its Two Ingredient Factors
sections.summary: gib_gelin_cesaro is stated, then the proof assembles the two ingredients: the parent's gib_cassini recentred at base n−1 (hA) and the gib_catalan r=2 instance at base n−2 (hB), with Int.fib 2 = 1 clearing the Fᵣ² factor. The sign lemma sign_flip aligns the parities: (−1)^|n−1| = −(−1)^|n| (hs1) and (−1)^|n−2| = (−1)^|n| (hs2), rewritten into hA and hB.
sections.mathContext: Cassini: G(n−1)G(n+1) = G(n)² + (−1)^|n|μ;  Catalan r=2: G(n−2)G(n+2) = G(n)² − (−1)^|n|μ.

sections.title: Difference of Squares and Conclusion
sections.summary: The two outer-product forms hP, hQ (symmetric about G(n)²) are extracted by linear_combination; he2 squares the sign factor away (((−1)^|n|)² = 1). A calc reorders the four-factor product into (G(n)²−s)(G(n)²+s) with s = (−1)^|n|μ, substitutes, and one linear_combination of he2 closes the goal at −μ².

sections.title: Fibonacci Specialisation
sections.summary: fib_gelin_cesaro: the seed (a,b) = (1,0) has μ = 1, so gib 1 0 = Int.fib and the master identity collapses (by simpa) to the classical F(n−2)F(n−1)F(n+1)F(n+2) − F(n)⁴ = −1.

sections.title: Lucas Specialisation
sections.summary: lucas_gelin_cesaro: the seed (a,b) = (1,2) has discriminant μ = −5, so (by norm_num + simpa [lucas]) L(n−2)L(n−1)L(n+1)L(n+2) − L(n)⁴ = −25 = −(−5)², the Lucas/√5 discriminant appearing squared.

crossReferences.description: Builds directly on the parent's gib_cassini, gib_catalan, sign_flip, gib, and lucas; completes the parent's Gibonacci lift by carrying the Gelin–Cesàro identity (which the parent proved only for Fibonacci) up to arbitrary Horadam sequences, with constant −μ²
The grandparent Vajda entry's Gelin–Cesàro open question is here generalised from the Fibonacci numbers to every Gibonacci sequence

conclusion.summary: Complete, fully verified (0 sorries, 0 axioms, no native_decide) proof of the Gibonacci Gelin–Cesàro identity G(n−2)G(n−1)G(n+1)G(n+2) − G(n)⁴ = −(a²−ab−b²)² for arbitrary integer Gibonacci (Horadam) sequences, with the Fibonacci (μ=1, −1) and Lucas (μ=−5, −25) specialisations.
conclusion.implications: Completes the parent entry's lift of the Fibonacci product hierarchy to Gibonacci sequences: the degree-four Gelin–Cesàro identity, like Cassini, Catalan, and Vajda before it, is governed by the single discriminant μ = a²−ab−b², appearing here squared. The Lucas constant −25 = −5² falls out automatically from the seeds (1, 2).
openQuestions: Prove the Gibonacci analogue of d'Ocagne's identity G(m)G(n+1) − G(m+1)G(n) = (−1)^|n|·μ·F(m−n) (still open from the parent).
Lift Gelin–Cesàro further to the full Horadam recurrence W(n+2) = pW(n+1) + qW(n), where the discriminant constant becomes a function of p, q and the seeds.
